composition_parti.note: Deliberately left open: the two members name two different, mutually exclusive symmetry classes in their own proportional_system.symmetry field (balanced-asymmetrical vs. additive-vernacular), and tuscan-vernacular's own c04 states that imposing symmetry on it 'converts the building into a villa' — i.e. into the other member. Neither reading is more 'the family' than the other; both are real and distinguish the two members from each other on purpose.
composition_parti.rule: Symmetry class is the primary thing that tells the two members apart and is resolved at the style level, not here.

variants.note: italian-villa-vernacular's own proportional_system.symmetry is literally 'balanced-asymmetrical'; its own c02 requires the tower off the centre line and taller than the block by at least 30% — a deliberate, composed asymmetry, not an accident.
tuscan-vernacular's own proportional_system.symmetry is literally 'additive-vernacular'; growth is by adding 4.0-4.5 m cells along the contour with no imposed rhythm.
tuscan-vernacular's own massing_affinities explicitly forbids this: 'the irregularity is a byproduct of accretion, never a composition... reads immediately as false here.'

roof_pitch.rule: Low-pitched throughout, roughly 3:12 to 6:12. italian-villa-vernacular's own hard constraint (c01) sets 3:12-5:12; tuscan-vernacular's own hard constraint (c03) sets 4:12-6:12. The two ranges overlap at 4:12-5:12; a roof outside the outer bound of 3:12-6:12 is outside the family in either member.

pitch_range.note: Union of the two members' own hard-constraint ranges; 4:12-5:12 is the overlap and the safest single value absent a style-level choice.

roof_material.rule: Low-fired clay roof tile throughout — coppi e embrici (half-round cap-and-pan), laid without underlayment in both members. No wood shingle, slate, or metal roofing appears in either style's own description.

eave_condition.rule: The eave projects well beyond the wall face — on paired brackets (modiglioni) in italian-villa-vernacular, on corbelled tile courses (gronda) in tuscan-vernacular — to throw a shadow line down the rendered wall and carry rainwater clear of it. The two members' own overhang dimensions barely overlap (villa 600-1200 mm on brackets; farm 300-600 mm on corbelled tile), so no single figure or bracket-vs-corbel choice is stated here — only the shared functional principle.

construction_type.rule: Load-bearing masonry throughout, rendered/limewashed or left as coursed stone — rubble limestone or mixed stone-and-brick in tuscan-vernacular (500-700 mm walls, 'the mass doing the thermal work'), rendered and limewashed mass masonry in italian-villa-vernacular. No light timber frame anywhere in the family; the wall is real structural mass in both members, not cladding over a frame.

variants.note: Neither member ever built primary walls in timber frame; wood appears only as floor/roof/loggia framing.

wall_thickness_masonry.rule: Wall thickness runs thick across the family, roughly 400 to 700 mm (16-28 in) depending on storey and member: tuscan-vernacular states 500-700 mm at ground reducing to 400-500 mm above; italian-villa-vernacular states 450-600 mm — both the direct expression of the same load-bearing rubble/mass-masonry construction.

thickness_range.note: Union of the two members' own stated ranges (tuscan-vernacular 400-700mm / 16-28in; italian-villa-vernacular 450-600mm / 18-24in) — a synthesized bracket, not a single measured figure.

reveal_masonry.rule: Openings are set deep into the thick wall, roughly 300 to 600 mm (12-24 in), so the wall reads as real mass rather than a thin veneer punched with holes. italian-villa-vernacular states 300-450 mm reveals; tuscan-vernacular's own hard constraint (c02) requires reveals of at least 350 mm and its typical_ratios give 400-600 mm.

reveal_depth.note: Union of both members' own stated reveal ranges.

cornice.rule: No applied classical (moulded stone) cornice occurs. The roofline in both members is finished by a functional bracketed or corbelled eave overhang, not a classical crown moulding — see `eave_condition` for the real detail. Neither member's text names 'cornice' directly; this redirect is an inference held at low confidence.

frieze.rule: No classical frieze band occurs, for the same reason as `cornice`: the family has no applied entablature to carry one. Held at low confidence for the same reason — neither member's text names 'frieze' directly.

order.rule: No graduated classical order (moulded base, fluted or enriched shaft, full entablature) appears anywhere in this family. italian-villa-vernacular's own c04 states 'no pediment and no applied order on the exterior'; tuscan-vernacular's own lineage note states plainly 'the order system is not inherited at all.' Where columns occur, see the `column` slot.

column.rule: Where a loggia or arcade occurs — the family's only columnar element — its columns (or piers) are plain and unfluted and carry a simple impost band directly, never a moulded capital-and-full-entablature combination, consistent with the family's own 'no applied order' rule. italian-villa-vernacular's own c04 states this explicitly ('unfluted Tuscan or Doric carrying an impost, not an entablature'); tuscan-vernacular's loggia piers (where present) are sized by span alone ('pier width 0.4-0.6 of the clear opening') with no order vocabulary at all.

entablature.rule: No classical entablature (architrave-frieze-cornice run) occurs anywhere in the family. Stated directly for italian-villa-vernacular (c04: loggia columns carry 'an impost, not an entablature'); tuscan-vernacular's loggia piers, where present, are sized by span alone with no order vocabulary at all.

pediment.rule: No pediment appears anywhere in the family. Stated directly for italian-villa-vernacular (c04: 'no pediment... on the exterior'); consistent with tuscan-vernacular's own description of a working farmhouse with openings 'placed by internal need rather than by facade rhythm' and 'no ornament.'

pilaster.rule: No applied pilaster order occurs. Neither member's own text names a pilaster specifically; this is inferred from italian-villa-vernacular's own broader rule ('no applied order on the exterior') and is marked as an inference, not a direct quotation, hence lower confidence than the `order` slot itself.

ornament_vocabulary.rule: Ornament is confined to what construction itself requires — an arch impost, an eaves bracket or corbel course, a chimney's tile cap — and is never applied decoratively for its own sake. This restates the family's own defining_characteristics verbatim: 'Ornament almost entirely absent, concentrated where it is unavoidable.'

daylight_strategy.rule: Small, deeply-reveal openings keep glazed area a low fraction of wall area, so thermal mass — not shading or ventilation — carries the cooling load. tuscan-vernacular's own hard constraint (c02) caps aperture area at 12 percent of any wall; italian-villa-vernacular's own typical_ratios run a little more generously, 12-20 percent. Both sit far below a light-frame style's typical glazing ratio.

orientation_rule.rule: The principal shaded outdoor room (the loggia, or the aia threshing floor) opens toward the sun's low-angle side. italian-villa-vernacular's own hard-adjacent constraint (c05) requires the loggia to face between southeast and southwest; tuscan-vernacular states the same siting descriptively rather than as a formal constraint ('shade trees on the south side'). The villa's figure is the better-documented of the two and is used here.

bearing_range.note: 0 = north. Directly from italian-villa-vernacular's own hard-adjacent constraint; tuscan-vernacular corroborates only descriptively.

landscape_idiom.rule: The house is inseparable from its working agricultural ground — terraced retaining walls and an axial approach in italian-villa-vernacular, the aia and contour-following siting in tuscan-vernacular — never a house with a designed ornamental garden read as a separate architectural work.
